unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2 of your Year 8 English course. At its centre is "Signal in the Static", an investigative story in which two student journalists, Imani and Kofi, follow an anonymous tip about a secret land deal that threatens their city's community gardens. Around the story you will study how design and packaging shape the messages we trust, and why sustainable communication matters as much as sustainable materials. You will master 30 vocabulary words about investigation, emotion and public life, make partitive expressions your primary grammar focus, and practise zero and first conditionals, relative clauses, comparatives and superlatives, formal questions beginning with prepositions, and the passive voice.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Compare evidence, viewpoint and source reliability. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise a cohesive multi-paragraph response. Present, defend, reflect and complete the quiz.

readings.title: Packaging the Truth: How Design Shapes What We Believe
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Every message you receive arrives in packaging. Before you weigh a single fact, someone has already chosen the colours, the fonts, the size of the headline, the photographs and the tone of voice. Designers call these choices presentation; readers rarely notice them at all. Yet those quiet choices steer what we believe, long before we ask whether a claim is actually true. Learning to see the package as well as the product is one of the most useful skills a young reader can build.
Consider two cartons of orange juice standing side by side on a market shelf. The juice inside is identical. One carton is plain, with a simple list of contents. The other glows with a painted sunrise, a smiling farmer and the luminous words "pure natural goodness". Nothing on the second carton is false, exactly, yet nothing is proven either. The design makes an implicit claim about health and honesty without stating anything a customer could challenge. Shoppers who want the facts must decipher the small print on the back, where the sugar content hides in letters three millimetres tall. The bright front of the box can even obstruct our attention, pulling our eyes away from the one panel that matters.
Sustainability raises the stakes. Wasteful packaging buries a small product in a multitude of layers: plastic film, moulded trays, ribbons and boxes inside boxes. Honest packaging does the opposite. It uses the least material the journey requires, shows the product truthfully and helps the buyer recycle every part. Good design can avert a great deal of waste before a single item is sold. When designers feign concern for the planet with green leaves and empty slogans, researchers call it greenwashing; when they redesign the package itself, rivers and beaches feel the difference.
Information behaves in exactly the same way. A sensational headline is bubble wrap for a thin story. An erratic stream of posts can inundate your feed until no single fact stands still long enough to be checked. Monotonous repetition is a package too: hear a claim ten times and it begins to feel true, though repetition adds not a drop of evidence. A narrative can be shaped, trimmed and wrapped exactly like a product, and a synopsis can hide as much as it reveals, depending on which details the writer selects. None of this makes design evil; it makes design powerful, and power deserves pertinent questions.
So how does a reader unwrap a message? Journalists suggest a short checklist of formal questions. From which source does this claim come? By whom was the photograph taken? For whose benefit was this message designed? About which facts is the message strangely silent? If a message cannot survive four calm questions, it does not deserve your trust. A piece of verified evidence is worth more than a surge of outrage, and careful analysis will always outlast a beautiful package.
The lesson of this unit is that sustainability applies to communication as much as to cardboard. Sustainable packaging avoids waste and shows the buyer the truth about what is inside; sustainable journalism avoids sensationalism and shows the reader the evidence behind every claim. Both trades flourish on the same raw material, which is trust, and trust is a resource that vanishes faster than any forest. Readers who ask pertinent questions, who refuse to let bright colours obstruct their judgement, and who take time to decipher what the package conceals, become very hard to fool. In the story that anchors this unit, two student journalists discover exactly how much courage that kind of reading requires when the package being sold to their city is a story about its gardens.

readings.title: On Air, On Record: An Interview with Producer Amara
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Amara produces the weekly youth programme at a community radio station, and she has spent four years turning nervous student volunteers into careful reporters. She is sociable in the corridor and strict in the studio, a combination her trainees seem to love. We spoke to her about how a small station protects a big thing: the truth. Her answers have been shortened for length, and every fact she mentions was checked against the station's public record.
Interviewer: From which sources do you gather your information each week?
Amara: We start with people, not posts. Market traders, nurses, drivers, gardeners; the people who feel a problem before anyone writes about it. Social media gives us leads, but a lead is not a fact. It is an invitation to check.
Interviewer: With whom do you check a difficult claim before it is broadcast?
Amara: Two independent sources, always. If a council officer tells us one thing, we look for a document, a record or a second person who knows the file. Our rule is simple, and we treat it like a law of nature: if we cannot verify a claim, we do not broadcast it. There are no exceptions on my desk.
Interviewer: About which mistakes do you warn new reporters most often?
Amara: Speed. If you rush a story, you will make mistakes, and one careless error can undo a year of careful work. I also warn them about officials who give oblique answers. An evasive speaker loves a vague question. A precise, formal question leaves an evasive speaker nowhere to hide, because it names exactly the information required. That is why we drill our trainees to ask questions that begin with the preposition: from which office, by whom, for whose benefit.
Interviewer: What happens when the station gets something wrong?
Amara: We say so on air, at the same hour, in the same slot. A correction is not a humiliation; it is restitution to the listener, giving back the accuracy we owe them. I would rather deliver one honest rebuke to my own programme than let a false detail flourish in a thousand conversations.
Interviewer: Young reporters can feel overwhelmed. What is your advice for the nervous ones?
Amara: Feeling nervous is evidence that you understand the responsibility. Before the microphone opens, I tell them to quell the shaking with slow breathing and a glass of water, and then to trust their preparation. The nerves never fully leave. Honestly, that is part of what makes live radio so exhilarating.
Interviewer: Some adults say young people should leave difficult stories alone. How do you respond?
Amara: I ask them a question back: if a story touches the buses young people ride and the parks where they play, to whom does that story belong? Young reporters are not a hindrance when they are trained. They notice what tired adults have stopped seeing. My job is to be adept at two things at once: protecting my trainees and refusing to let anyone usurp their right to ask.
Interviewer: What should a listener do with a rumour they hear at the market?
Amara: Treat it like an unripe mango. Do not swallow it, and do not throw it away. Bring it to someone who can test it. If listeners send us a rumour with a name, a place and a date, we can work; if they send us a surge of anger and nothing else, we cannot. Evidence is the kindest gift an audience can give.

readings.title: Signal in the Static, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Imani adjusted her headphones and leaned into the microphone. "This is Horizon Youth Radio, news and truth from the city's students, for the city's future. I am Imani. Let us begin." Behind the glass, Kofi gave her a thumbs-up, and the red LIVE light glowed steadily against the studio wall.
They had been running the school radio station for almost a year. What began as a journalism-class project had grown into a respected youth platform: they had covered water shortages and examination protests, and they had even produced a careful segment about restitution for families displaced by the floods. Now something new was unfolding, and it felt bigger than anything they had faced before.
It began with a message slipped under the radio-room door. No name. No signature. "They are lying. What you are hearing about the city gardens is fake. There is more beneath the soil than plants."
Kofi thought it was a joke. "Someone is trying to be dramatic," he said, spinning the paper across the desk. Imani, however, did not dismiss it. The handwriting was neat, and the language was calculated rather than emotional. Oblique, even; suggestive, but never direct. Whoever wrote it wanted to be followed, not caught. "I want to know more," she said.
Later that week a new narrative emerged online: photographs of council trucks parked at the northern edge of the public gardens. Some people claimed the land was being sold to private developers. Others insisted it was routine renovation. The official synopsis from the mayor's office promised new irrigation pipelines and community gardens ready to flourish. Yet no plans had been released, no engineers were named and no contractors were listed. Just noise, arranged to sound like an answer.
So they investigated. They interviewed gardeners, market sellers and a retired city planner, and almost nobody had heard anything official. One vendor near the garden gate lowered her voice to a whisper. "They say a stranger came with contracts and big money. But the families living beside the gardens were told nothing."
Imani felt a surge of indignation rise in her chest. "Why would nobody announce it?"
"Because," the woman said, folding her scarf slowly, "some of us would fight back."
At school, Imani arranged an interview with the deputy mayor's aide, a tall, calm man named Mr. Nadir, who wore an impassive expression from the first question to the last.
"So the city's plans for the gardens are public?" Imani asked.
He smiled faintly. "Of course."
"May we see them?"
"They are being updated. The full report will be available next month."
Kofi glanced at Imani. A delay. Convenient.
"Some residents say nearby families are being pressured to move. Quietly."
"That is incorrect," Mr. Nadir said smoothly. "Those are baseless rumours."
"Then who started the rumours?" Imani pressed.
His expression did not move at all. "That is not pertinent."
Back at school, the debate club hosted a special event: should young people intervene in public policy? Imani presented her argument first. "If we do not ask questions, adults will write the future without us. We must intervene, investigate, and demand clarity."
A student named Arjun disagreed just as firmly. "We are not experts. If we get involved in everything, we will only create confusion. Youth action can be a hindrance, not a help."
Kofi spoke next. "But what if we are the only ones who notice what the adults have missed?"
Imani closed with quiet power. "Sometimes we must quell our own fear in order to question authority, especially when silence is exactly what someone wants."
That night, Kofi was editing the next episode when his computer stuttered and went dark. The garden files had vanished; only static remained on the timeline. "Someone accessed the system," he told Imani, his voice shaking. "They wiped everything."
She stared at the empty screen. "That is not a mistake. That is a warning."
Then came the call. A man's voice, masked and modulated. "Stop pushing. You are students. Do not make this worse for people you care about."
Imani's throat tightened around one question. "And if we keep going?"

readings.title: Signal in the Static, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
"Then you will forfeit more than files." The line went dead, and the studio felt suddenly very small.
Kofi sat down slowly. "This is serious now. If we keep digging, we could get into real trouble, and not only with the school."
"But if we stop," Imani said, "we let them usurp the truth. It becomes theirs to shape, theirs to bury."
She looked around their tiny studio: the old microphones, the battered table, the wall where vines climbed from a chipped pot and sent out delicate tendrils toward the light. The room felt quiet, monotonous almost, yet beneath the stillness pulsed a choice that would not wait for morning.
"I say we go live tomorrow," she said at last. "Not with conclusions. Just with questions."
Kofi breathed out, then nodded. "All right. Questions."
The next day they went on air. "Today's episode is different," Imani began. "We will not tell you what is true. We will tell you what we found, and you will decide for yourselves."
They played their interviews, quoted the vendors and described the files that had disappeared overnight. They even aired a short segment titled "From which perspective is the garden story being told?", a plain lesson in bias and source-checking for every listener with a radio.
"We are not accusing anyone," Kofi said carefully. "We are asking why so many answers have gone dark at the same time."
As they wrapped up, the studio line lit and would not stop. A multitude of calls inundated the little switchboard. "I am a teacher," said one voice. "I have heard the same rumours for weeks. Thank you for speaking up." Another caller said quietly, "I work at the city hall. You are not wrong."
Imani exulted, but silently. No cheering, no fists in the air; just one long breath and a private moment of pride.
The response came within days. The station's power cut out during the morning slot, and the school administration blamed a tired generator. Students began receiving fake emails claiming the station was shutting down. A few teachers suggested, kindly and not so kindly, that the pair had gone too far. "You are students," one said. "Stay in your lane."
They did not stop. Imani wrote a piece for the school paper titled "Who Decides What Is Pertinent?", and she chose the passive voice deliberately, so that no source could be traced through her sentences. "The gardens were promised. The questions were raised. The files were deleted. And the truth? Still unclear." Readers noticed what was missing from every sentence: the names of whoever had done the promising, the deleting and the deciding.
A week later came the turning point. A new envelope appeared in Kofi's locker, anonymous again, but heavier. Inside was a scanned analysis of land permits carrying signatures from the mayor's office and a private firm. The garden land had been leased, quietly, with no community vote and no consultation of the families beside it.
"We need to decipher this," Imani said, her heart pounding. "Every line, every signature, every date."
They did. Then they aired a new show, with no shouting and no speculation; only evidence, read slowly. They used comparatives to lay the conflicting accounts side by side: "One version is louder, another quieter. One is cleaner, the other more erratic."
"But truth," Imani ended, "is not always the most luminous. Sometimes it hides in whispers until someone asks the right question."
The city responded at last. An official investigation began, the deputy mayor resigned, and some families received formal apologies and early restitution for what had been taken from them.
They were not heroes, and they knew it. At the year-end ceremony, Imani was invited to read a message to the whole school. She said simply, "Young people are not a hindrance. We are a mirror. We reflect what adults refuse to see."
The crowd stood and applauded; not everyone, but enough. She and Kofi did not feel triumphant. They felt steady, which was better. It was the kind of joy you do not shout about. The kind you earn.

comprehension.question: According to 'Packaging the Truth', which choices has someone already made before you weigh a single fact in a message?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Someone has already chosen the colours, the fonts, the size of the headline, the photographs and the tone of voice.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored to the opening paragraph's list of presentation choices that steer belief before facts are examined.

comprehension.question: In the interview, what is Amara's unbreakable rule about claims, and how many independent sources does she require?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Her rule is that if the station cannot verify a claim, it does not broadcast it, and every difficult claim needs two independent sources.
comprehension.explanation: A retrieval question anchored to Amara's answers about checking claims with two sources and her law-like verification rule.

comprehension.question: What did the anonymous note slipped under the radio-room door claim about the city gardens?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It claimed the official story about the gardens was fake and warned that there was more beneath the soil than plants.
comprehension.explanation: A literal recall question anchored to the quoted wording of the anonymous message in the story's opening chapters.

comprehension.question: What evidence finally proved that the garden land had been leased, and where did it appear?
comprehension.correctAnswer: A scanned analysis of land permits, signed by the mayor's office and a private firm, appeared anonymously in Kofi's locker.
comprehension.explanation: A literal recall question anchored to the turning-point scene where the envelope of permits reaches Kofi's locker.

comprehension.question: How does the sunrise juice carton make an implicit health claim, and why is that claim so difficult to challenge?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Its painted sunrise, smiling farmer and the words about natural goodness suggest health without stating any checkable fact, so there is nothing a customer can disprove.
comprehension.explanation: An inference question anchored to the two-carton example, testing the passage's definition of an implicit claim.

comprehension.question: According to Amara, what does a precise, formal question achieve when a speaker is being evasive?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She says a precise, formal question leaves an evasive speaker nowhere to hide, because it names exactly the information required.
comprehension.explanation: A vocabulary-in-context question anchored to Amara's advice about oblique answers and preposition-first questions.

comprehension.question: What do Mr. Nadir's impassive expression and his reply 'That is not pertinent' suggest about his attitude to the students' questions?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He keeps himself deliberately unreadable and dismisses the question about who started the rumours, suggesting he wants to control what counts as relevant and reveal nothing.
comprehension.explanation: A feelings-with-evidence question anchored to the interview scene, linking two quoted details to a judgement about character.

comprehension.question: Why does Imani deliberately choose the passive voice for her article 'Who Decides What Is Pertinent?'
comprehension.correctAnswer: The passive voice lets her report the promises, deletions and unanswered questions without naming anyone, so her sources stay protected and the missing doers become the message.
comprehension.explanation: A writer's-craft question anchored to the article scene, testing why the by-phrases are missing from her sentences.

comprehension.question: Explain the comparison 'Packaging the Truth' draws between sustainable packaging and sustainable journalism.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Sustainable packaging avoids waste and shows the buyer the truth about the contents, and sustainable journalism likewise avoids sensationalism and shows the reader the evidence, because both depend on trust.
comprehension.explanation: A synthesis question anchored to the closing paragraphs, requiring both halves of the analogy and the shared idea of trust.

comprehension.question: Amara says, 'If we cannot verify a claim, we do not broadcast it.' How does this zero conditional sum up her standard of journalism?
comprehension.correctAnswer: By phrasing the rule like a law of nature that is always true, she shows verification is not a preference but an unchanging condition for anything reaching the air.
comprehension.explanation: A language-analysis question anchored to Amara's quoted rule, connecting the grammar of the zero conditional to its meaning.

comprehension.question: Summarise the debate between Imani and Arjun, giving one argument each speaker uses.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Imani argues that young people must intervene and ask questions or adults will write the future without them, while Arjun argues that students are not experts and youth action can be a hindrance that creates confusion.
comprehension.explanation: A comparison question anchored to the debate-club scene, requiring one accurate point from each side of the motion.

comprehension.question: What does Imani mean by refusing to let anyone 'usurp the truth', and how does her closing mirror image answer Arjun's earlier argument?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means officials would seize control of the story without any right to it if the students stayed silent, and her line that young people are a mirror, not a hindrance, directly overturns Arjun's word from the debate.
comprehension.explanation: An evaluation question anchored to part 2's decision scene and ceremony speech, linking usurp and the mirror line back to the debate.

grammar.title: Partitive Expressions
grammar.explanation: Partitive expressions name a portion of something, so instead of vague sentences like "I want cake" or "She felt happiness" you can say "I want a piece of cake" or "She felt a surge of happiness." They matter most with uncountable nouns such as water, information and excitement, which cannot take a number on their own.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A partitive expression is a measure word plus of placed before a noun: a piece of + cake = a piece of cake.
Step 1 - decide whether the noun is countable (apple/apples) or uncountable (water, information, sugar; you cannot say two waters or three informations).
Step 2 - choose the partitive that fits the noun: a piece of (cake, advice, information, evidence); a glass of (water, juice, milk); a cup of (tea, coffee, soup); a slice of (bread, pizza, cake); a bit of (help, luck, sugar); a drop of (water, rain, oil); a lot of (time, money, students); a surge of (excitement, anger, energy); a multitude of (people, reasons, problems); a handful of (nuts, coins, students); a bunch of (flowers, grapes, keys).
Step 3 - with countable plurals you can also use a few (I have a few friends in this class.), a couple of (She bought a couple of books.) and several (There are several reasons for this decision.).
Step 4 - with uncountable nouns use a little (Add a little sugar to the tea.), a bit of (I need a bit of advice.) and a great deal of (There is a great deal of information to process.).
Story link: when Imani feels a surge of indignation, and a multitude of calls inundates the studio, the author is using partitives to measure emotion and scale precisely.
grammar.commonMistake: Three traps catch most writers. First, pairing the wrong partitive with the noun: water cannot be cut, so a piece of water fails where a glass of water or a drop of water works. Second, dropping the partitive entirely, which leaves bare, vague sentences such as "I want cake." Third, reaching for a lot of when a sharper measure exists: a surge of excitement says far more than a lot of excitement.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of partitives as sharing words that cut a whole into servings: if you can count the noun, serve it with a few or a couple of; if you cannot count it, pour it with a bit of or a little.
grammar.practice:
Part A - choose the correct partitive for each sentence: 1) Can I have ______ (a piece of / a few) cake? 2) Pour me ______ (a cup of / a couple of) tea, please. 3) I need ______ (a little / a bunch) help with my homework. 4) She wants ______ (a slice of / a drop of) pizza. 5) There is ______ (a lot of / a few) excitement in the room! 6) Only ______ (a handful of / a glass of) students passed the difficult exam. 7) After the announcement, there was ______ (a surge of / a slice of) indignation among the community. 8) He ate ______ (a bit of / a multitude of) bread for breakfast.
Part B - write your own sentence for each partitive, keeping it true to your own life: a surge of; a multitude of; a handful of; a piece of; a bit of; a drop of.

grammar.title: Zero and First Conditionals
grammar.explanation: Conditionals describe what happens, or what will happen, if a condition is met. The zero conditional states facts that are always true, while the first conditional predicts real future possibilities the speaker genuinely expects.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Zero conditional - facts and general truths. Structure: If + present simple, present simple. Examples: If you heat ice, it melts. If you mix red and blue, you get purple. If it rains, the grass gets wet. If plants do not get water, they die. Because the result always follows, when can replace if: When you heat ice, it melts.
First conditional - real future possibilities. Structure: If + present simple, will + base verb. Examples: If I study hard, I will pass the test. If it rains tomorrow, I will bring an umbrella. If we intervene now, we will avert disaster. If you feign calm, they will push harder.
Softer results swap will for might or can: If I finish my homework, I might play outside. If you ask politely, she can help you.
Story link: the choice in the studio is argued entirely in conditionals. Kofi warns, "If we keep digging, we could get into real trouble," and Imani answers, "If we stop, we let them usurp the truth."
grammar.commonMistake: The classic error is planting will inside the if-clause: "If you will study hard, you will pass" should be "If you study hard, you will pass," because the if-clause stays in the present simple. Writers also blur the two types: "If you heat water, it boils" states a permanent fact, while "If you heat the water, I will make tea" promises one specific future action.
grammar.memoryTip: Zero is a law of nature that never switches off, so both halves stay in the present; first is one real fork in your future, so listen for the will in the result.
grammar.practice:
Part A - label each sentence zero or first: 1) If you drop a ball, it falls. 2) If it snows tomorrow, we will build a snowman. 3) If you press the button, the door opens. 4) If Imani investigates the story, she will uncover the truth. 5) If water reaches 100 degrees, it boils.
Part B - complete each sentence with the correct verb forms: 6) If you ______ (study) every day, you ______ (improve) your English. (First) 7) If water ______ (freeze), it ______ (turn) to ice. (Zero) 8) If we ______ (leave) now, we ______ (arrive) on time. (First) 9) If you ______ (not water) plants, they ______ (die). (Zero) 10) If she ______ (practise) speaking, she ______ (become) more confident. (First)
Part C - write one zero and one first conditional about the radio station's next broadcast.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses
grammar.explanation: A relative clause adds information about a noun, introduced by who for people, that for things or people, which for things, and whose for possession. Choosing between defining and non-defining clauses, and punctuating them correctly, is what separates precise writing from confusing writing.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Step 1 - find the noun you want to expand. Step 2 - choose the pronoun: who (people), that (things or people), which (things), whose (possession). Step 3 - attach the extra information straight after the pronoun. Step 4 - check the commas.
Defining clauses carry essential information and take no commas: The student who won the debate is in my class. The document that contained the permits was anonymous. Remove the clause and you no longer know which student or which document.
Non-defining clauses add extra, removable information and sit between commas: Imani, who runs the radio station, is very brave. The radio station, which was started as a school project, became a trusted voice in the city.
Whose shows belonging for people and things alike: The plant, whose tendrils flourished in the light, grew taller every day.
Story link: one comma changes the meaning. "My brother who enjoys maths is revising" implies several brothers; "My brother, who enjoys maths, is revising" describes the only one.
grammar.commonMistake: Two habits cause most marks lost. Using which for a person: "The teacher which helped us" must become "The teacher who helped us." And dropping the commas around a non-defining clause: writing "My brother who enjoys maths is studying" when you have one brother accidentally claims you have a spare.
grammar.memoryTip: People get who, things get which, that is the flexible spare for defining work, and whose hands over the keys of ownership; commas are the hug you give information the sentence could live without.
grammar.practice:
Part A - fill each blank with who, that, which or whose: 1) The girl ______ won the race is my friend. 2) I have a book ______ is very interesting. 3) The teacher ______ helps us is very kind. 4) The flowers, ______ are blooming, smell wonderful. 5) The argument ______ he presented was flawed. 6) The plant, ______ tendrils flourished in the light, grew taller every day.
Part B - combine each pair using a relative clause: 7) Kofi edits audio. Kofi is Imani's partner at the radio station. 8) The message was anonymous. The message started the investigation. 9) Mr. Nadir gave evasive answers. Mr. Nadir works for the deputy mayor. 10) The gardens are threatened. The gardens are in the northern part of the city.
Part C - decide which of your four combined sentences needed commas, and explain why in one line.

grammar.title: Questions Beginning with Prepositions
grammar.explanation: Formal English can lift a preposition from the end of a question to the very front, turning "Which perspective was the story told from?" into "From which perspective was the story told?" The fronted form sounds polished, academic and precise, which is why interviewers and examiners favour it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Step 1 - find the preposition hiding at the end of the informal question (from, with, to, about, for). Step 2 - move it to the front. Step 3 - follow it with the question word: which, whom or what (after a preposition, who becomes whom). Step 4 - keep the rest of the word order unchanged.
Paired examples: Which store did you buy that from? -> From which store did you buy that? Who did you give the book to? -> To whom did you give the book? What topic is your presentation about? -> About what topic is your presentation? Who are you going to the party with? -> With whom are you going to the party?
Story link: Imani builds an entire broadcast segment around one fronted question, "From which perspective is the garden story being told?", and Amara trains her reporters to ask from which office, by whom and for whose benefit, because a precise question leaves an evasive speaker nowhere to hide.
grammar.commonMistake: Keeping the preposition in both places at once: "From which teacher do you like learning from?" doubles the from, and only the front copy should survive. The other slip is writing who directly after a preposition; formal grammar requires whom, as in "To whom did you address the letter?"
grammar.memoryTip: Lift the little word to the front of the queue and let whom fall in politely behind it; if you can hear the preposition twice, one of them is trespassing.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each question with the preposition at the front: 1) Which teacher do you like learning from? 2) Which country did this package come from? 3) Which friend are you going to the library with? 4) Which issue is the article about? 5) Which person did you address the letter to?
Challenge - draft two fronted questions of your own that you could put to a city official about the garden story.

grammar.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.explanation: Comparatives weigh two things against each other, while superlatives crown the highest or lowest degree among three or more. The form depends on the length of the adjective, plus a short list of irregulars every writer simply memorises.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Comparative forms: one syllable adds -er (tall -> taller, fast -> faster); one syllable ending in -e adds -r (large -> larger, nice -> nicer); consonant-vowel-consonant doubles the final letter (big -> bigger, hot -> hotter); two syllables ending in -y swap y for i (happy -> happier, easy -> easier); longer adjectives take more (careful -> more careful, beautiful -> more beautiful).
Superlative forms mirror them with -est and most: tallest, largest, biggest, happiest, most careful.
Irregulars: good -> better -> best; bad -> worse -> worst; far -> farther or further -> farthest or furthest; little -> less -> least; much and many -> more -> most.
Story link: Imani lays the conflicting accounts side by side with comparatives - "One version is louder, another quieter. One is cleaner, the other more erratic." - and closes with a superlative warning that truth "is not always the most luminous."
grammar.commonMistake: Doubling the marking is the trap to avoid: "more louder" and "most fastest" each carry two comparisons where one belongs, so choose either the ending or the helper word. Writers also reach for a comparative when three or more things are being ranked; among the whole class, someone is the most determined, not the more determined.
grammar.memoryTip: Two things compare with -er or more; three or more crown one champion with -est or most, and the champion always wears the.
grammar.practice:
Part A - write the correct form: 1) My brother is ______ (funny) than my sister. 2) Today is the ______ (cold) day of the year. 3) This book is ______ (interesting) than that one. 4) She is the ______ (good) student in the class. 5) The second film was ______ (bad) than the first. 6) Of all the planets, Jupiter is the ______ (large).
Part B - using the story, write three sentences comparing the official statement with the vendors' account; use one comparative with -er, one with more, and one superlative.

grammar.title: Passive Voice
grammar.explanation: The passive voice moves the focus from who performed an action to what was done, using a form of be plus the past participle. Writers choose it when the doer is unknown or unimportant, or when hiding the doer is itself the point.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Step 1 - find the object of the active sentence (what receives the action). Step 2 - promote that object to subject. Step 3 - add the right form of be: is/are for present, was/were for past. Step 4 - add the past participle of the main verb. Step 5 - attach by + doer only if the doer matters. Active: The teacher read the book. Passive: The book was read by the teacher.
Tense patterns: present simple, The report is written every week; past simple, The files were deleted; future simple, The project will be completed tomorrow; present continuous, The road is being repaired; past continuous, The letter was being written.
Story link: Imani's article runs on deliberate passives - "The gardens were promised. The questions were raised. The files were deleted." - so that no source can be traced through her sentences. The missing by-phrases are the whole message: nobody knows who promised, raised or deleted, and that mystery is her strategic writing choice.
grammar.commonMistake: Watch the two moving parts. The be-verb must carry the tense: "The book is read yesterday" needs was because the action is finished. And the main verb must be a true past participle: "The letter was wrote by my friend" needs written, since wrote is only the simple past.
grammar.memoryTip: Turn the spotlight around: the receiver of the action steps forward, be plus past participle carries the verb, and the doer either follows by or slips quietly out of the sentence.
grammar.practice:
Part A - rewrite each sentence in the passive voice: 1) The chef baked the cake. 2) Someone stole my bicycle. 3) The students completed the project. 4) The wind destroyed the old building. 5) Imani wrote the article.
Part B - label each sentence active or passive: 6) The message was deciphered by the students. 7) Kofi edited the audio files. 8) The land permits were signed by the mayor. 9) Imani broadcast the truth to the city. 10) The investigation was launched after the broadcast.
Part C - take two of your passive rewrites and delete the by-phrase, then note in one line how the effect changes.

No explanation has been offered so far."

writing.title: Writing 1: Persuasive Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a persuasive paragraph of 100 to 150 words arguing for or against this statement: "Young people should be allowed to investigate and report on public policy issues." Include a clear topic sentence stating your position, at least two partitive expressions (a piece of evidence, a multitude of reasons), at least one zero or first conditional, at least one relative clause, and a strong concluding sentence that reinforces your argument.
writing.modelText: Young people should be allowed to investigate public issues, because a multitude of decisions made today will shape the world they inherit. Student reporters who check their facts offer a piece of evidence where rumour offers only noise. If young journalists verify every claim, their broadcasts will strengthen the whole community rather than confuse it. Silence, which some adults quietly prefer, protects nobody. Give young reporters training and standards, and they will repay the trust.
writing.sentenceStarter: Young people deserve a place in public decisions because...
writing.expectedLength: One persuasive paragraph of 100 to 150 words
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: List your position, three reasons and the four required grammar features before you draft a single sentence.
writing.extension: Add a counterargument you take seriously, then rebut it in two further sentences without weakening your position.

writing.title: Writing 2: News Report in Passive Voice
writing.promptAndInstructions: As a journalist covering the events of "Signal in the Static", write a short news report of 80 to 120 words using the passive voice in at least five sentences. Cover the anonymous message, the investigation, the deleted files, the broadcast and the outcome, and keep every accusation out of your copy. Opening you may adapt: "An anonymous message was discovered at Horizon Youth Radio. An investigation was launched by two student journalists."
writing.modelText: An anonymous message was discovered at Horizon Youth Radio last month. An investigation was launched by two student journalists, and residents near the public gardens were interviewed. Days later, the station's files were deleted overnight, and a threatening call was received. The findings were broadcast without accusations, and dozens of calls were logged within the hour. A scanned set of land permits was then delivered anonymously, an official investigation was opened, and early restitution was granted to several families.
writing.sentenceStarter: An anonymous message was discovered at...
writing.expectedLength: Two news paragraphs of 80 to 120 words in total
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: Draft each event as an active sentence first, then convert it: object forward, be plus past participle, doer kept only if it is known.
writing.extension: Write a final paragraph in the active voice and compare aloud how the responsibility suddenly returns to the sentence.

writing.title: Writing 3: Comparative Essay
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short essay of 150 to 200 words comparing two characters from "Signal in the Static": Imani and Kofi, Imani and Arjun, or Imani and Mr. Nadir. Use comparatives and superlatives throughout. Consider who is more courageous, who is more cautious, who has the strongest argument in the debate scene, and who is the most important character in the story overall.
writing.modelText: Imani and Kofi make an effective team precisely because they differ. Imani is bolder and quicker to act, while Kofi is calmer and more careful with evidence. When the files vanish, Kofi is the more shaken of the two, yet his caution proves wiser than it first appears. Imani gives the loudest lines, but the strongest argument may belong to the vendor whose whisper started everything. Of everyone in the story, Imani remains the most determined, and that determination, more than courage or luck, is what finally forces the city to answer.
writing.sentenceStarter: The two characters differ most clearly in...
writing.expectedLength: Three cohesive paragraphs of 150 to 200 words
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: Build a two-column table of traits with one quotation per character before drafting your comparison.
writing.extension: Add a third character to one paragraph so that a superlative becomes genuinely necessary rather than decorative.

writing.title: Writing 4: Reflective Journal Entry
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a reflective journal entry of 100 to 150 words about a time you had to make a difficult decision. Use at least five vocabulary words from this unit and at least two different grammar structures from it, such as a partitive expression and a relative clause. Cover the situation, your options, your feelings, your decision and what you learned from the outcome.
writing.modelText: Last term I discovered that a poster competition entry, which a close friend had submitted, copied most of its design from a website. I felt a surge of worry rather than indignation. If I reported it, I would hurt someone I liked; if I stayed impassive, the contest became a small lie. I chose to talk to my friend first, and she withdrew the entry herself. The decision felt monotonous to explain and exhilarating to survive, and it taught me that honesty can intervene gently before adults ever need to.
writing.sentenceStarter: The decision I still think about began when...
writing.expectedLength: Two reflective paragraphs of 100 to 150 words
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: Choose your five vocabulary words first and pin each one to a specific moment in your story before drafting.
writing.extension: Rewrite your final sentence three ways: one conditional, one passive, one with a non-defining relative clause, then keep the best.

writing.title: Writing 5: Formal Letter of Inquiry
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a formal letter to a city office requesting information about a local project that affects young people, such as a park upgrade or a library schedule. Include at least three formal questions beginning with prepositions (From which..., To whom..., About what...), one partitive expression, a polite opening that explains who you are, and a closing line that requests a written reply by a specific date.
writing.modelText: Dear Projects Office, I am a Year 8 student researching the planned changes to Riverside Park for our school radio programme. From which budget will the upgrade be funded? With whom was the design contract signed? About what timetable should residents expect construction to run? Our listeners have a great deal of interest in this project, and a piece of official information would end much speculation. I would be grateful for a written reply by 15 September. Yours faithfully, A. Student.
writing.sentenceStarter: Dear Projects Office, I am writing to request...
writing.expectedLength: Three short paragraphs in formal letter layout
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: Note your three questions informally first, then move each preposition to the front and check whom follows it where needed.
writing.extension: Draft the office's evasive reply, then annotate it, marking every oblique phrase a careful reader should question.

writing.title: Writing 6: Connected Paragraph
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write one connected paragraph of six sentences explaining the biggest idea you are taking from this unit. Begin with a clear topic sentence, include one relative clause and one conditional sentence, join your ideas with connectives such as and, but, because and however, and end with a sentence that looks forward to how you will use the idea.
writing.modelText: The idea I am keeping from this unit is that every message arrives in packaging. Designers choose colours and headlines before we ever meet the facts, and those choices quietly steer our trust. The story of Imani and Kofi, which begins with one anonymous note, shows how much courage unwrapping a message can take. If I question the package before the product, I will judge information by its evidence rather than its shine. That habit matters because rumours travel faster than corrections. From now on, I plan to ask who designed each message and for whose benefit.
writing.sentenceStarter: The idea I am keeping from this unit is...
writing.expectedLength: One connected paragraph of six sentences
writing.successCriteria: I sustained a clear line of thought; shaped writing for audience and purpose; integrated precise vocabulary and attributed evidence; compared viewpoints and source reliability; used cohesive devices and varied structures; revised content and accuracy
writing.support: Sketch the six sentence jobs in order - claim, reason, example, condition, consequence, look-ahead - then write one sentence per job.
writing.extension: Compress your paragraph into a two-sentence synopsis without losing the relative clause or the conditional.

quizzes.question: In this unit, what does the verb 'usurp' mean?
quizzes.options: To flood or overwhelm a place or a person with an extremely large amount of something. | To take control of something, especially power, without the right to do so. | To speak angrily to someone because they have done something wrong. | To prevent something bad or dangerous from happening to someone.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To take control of something, especially power, without the right to do so.
quizzes.explanation: Usurp means to seize a role or power that does not belong to you, which is why Imani warns that staying silent lets officials usurp the truth.

quizzes.question: Which definition matches the adjective 'oblique'?
quizzes.options: Boring because it stays exactly the same and never changes. | Giving off light; bright or shining in the dark. | Very skilled or naturally talented at doing something. | Not straight or direct; slanted or angled.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Not straight or direct; slanted or angled.
quizzes.explanation: Oblique describes a line or a message that approaches at a slant, like the anonymous note that hints at wrongdoing without stating it.

quizzes.question: What does the noun 'restitution' mean?
quizzes.options: The act of giving back something that was lost or taken away. | A short summary of a story that gives only the main points. | A very large and sometimes uncountable number of people or things. | The slow and careful process of studying something closely to understand it better.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The act of giving back something that was lost or taken away.
quizzes.explanation: Restitution is repayment for what was taken; in the story, some families finally receive early restitution after the investigation begins.

quizzes.question: Mr. Nadir wore an 'impassive' expression during the interview. What does 'impassive' mean?
quizzes.options: Feeling very excited and thrilled by dramatic events. | Directly related to the topic that is currently under discussion. | Showing no emotion or feeling; calm and controlled. | Unpredictable and constantly changing without any clear pattern.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Showing no emotion or feeling; calm and controlled.
quizzes.explanation: Impassive means giving nothing away; Mr. Nadir keeps his face unreadable so the students cannot tell what he knows.

quizzes.question: Which sentence is a zero conditional expressing a general truth?
quizzes.options: If Imani investigates, she will uncover the truth. | If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils. | If we broadcast tomorrow, listeners will phone the station. | If you ask politely, the librarian might help you.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.
quizzes.explanation: The zero conditional keeps both halves in the present simple because the result always follows; the other options predict future possibilities with will or might.

quizzes.question: Which sentence uses a relative pronoun correctly?
quizzes.options: The teacher which helped us with revision is very kind. | The document who contained the permits was anonymous. | The student who won the debate is in my class. | My brother who enjoys maths, is studying tonight.
quizzes.correctAnswer: The student who won the debate is in my class.
quizzes.explanation: People take who and things take that or which; the first two options swap them, and the fourth strands a single comma where a pair or none belongs.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from 'Signal in the Static, part 1': "We must _____, investigate, and demand clarity."
